name: The Son of the Tree That Owns Itself

location.address: Corner of South Finley Street and Dearing Street, Athens, Georgia

access: Free. Stands on a public street corner in downtown Athens, visible and reachable at any time, no fee.
transport: Downtown Athens, Georgia. Athens is not currently one of our published US cities; this stands alone unless/until an Athens page exists.
story: This oak is the son of a tree that, by local legend, owned itself. The Athens Weekly Banner ran the story in 1890: Colonel William H. Jackson, fond of the white oak he had played under as a boy, deeded the tree ownership of itself and of the land within eight feet of its trunk. Legal scholars have picked holes in it ever since, on the reasonable ground that a tree cannot hold property, and Athens has never much minded. The original came down in a windstorm in 1942. On 4 December 1946 the Junior Ladies Garden Club planted a seedling raised from one of its acorns in the same plot, five feet tall and trimmed back to three for the move, with University of Georgia horticulture students turning the soil. It passed fifty feet by 2006. So the tree on the corner of South Finley and Dearing is about eighty years old rather than two hundred, and what it inherited was an acorn and a deed. Read it that way and it gets better rather than worse: the legend belongs to a tree that fell, and this one carries the name and the plot. A historical marker stands at the corner. There is no gate, no fee and no opening hours, and by the terms of a will nobody has ever tested in court, no landlord either.

name: Lover's Oak

location.address: Intersection of Albany Street and Prince Street, Brunswick Old Town Historic District, Brunswick, Georgia
location.neighbourhood: Standing in the middle of Albany Street, just south of Prince Street, in the historic downtown

access: Free, on a public street in downtown Brunswick, visible and reachable at any time.
transport: No public transit needed; in central Brunswick, GA, walkable from downtown.
story: Brunswick built its street around this oak instead of through it. Lover's Oak stands in the middle of Albany Street just south of Prince Street, ten main limbs branching low off one trunk, with the asphalt splitting and rejoining on either side of it. The city and Wikipedia both date it to the twelfth century, about nine hundred years, with no ring count or growth rate behind the number, so read that as the figure Brunswick has always used rather than anything measured. The trunk is cited at thirteen feet through, which is large enough for a live oak to be worth doubting; heavy buttressing at the base flatters a tape. What is not in doubt is what standing in a road costs. In 2015 a semi-truck hit the tree and tore off one of the ten limbs. It recovered, and traffic still goes around it. Southern live oaks are evergreen, swapping old leaves for new in spring without ever going bare, so there is no month to wait for and nothing to miss. It stands free and unfenced in the Old Town historic district, reachable at any hour, two blocks from the middle of downtown. The reason to walk those two blocks is not that it is the oldest thing in coastal Georgia. It is that a town rerouted itself around one tree and has never got round to changing its mind.

name: The Brandywine Sycamore (Lafayette Sycamore)

location.address: Beside the Gideon Gilpin House, Brandywine Battlefield Park, Baltimore Pike area, Chadds Ford, PA 19317
location.neighbourhood: Brandywine Battlefield Park, Chadds Ford Township, Delaware County

access: Free to view from the grounds; the Gideon Gilpin House itself is seen only on a timed guided tour (park operating as of 2023 visitor reviews, open Thu-Sun). The tree stands outside the house on the park grounds.
transport: No public transit found; car only. Roughly 40 km / 45-60 minutes by road from central Philadelphia, over the ~30-minute public-transport day-trip threshold, so this is its own place (Chadds Ford, PA) rather than folded into Philadelphia.
story: This sycamore was already 168 years old on the day the Battle of Brandywine broke around it. That figure comes from Union County College, which raised a seedling from its seed in 1997 and recorded the parent at 220 inches around, 111 feet tall and dating from about 1609. On 11 September 1777 the fighting ran through these fields, and the Marquis de Lafayette, nineteen years old and shot through the leg, was carried into the Gideon Gilpin farmhouse the tree stands beside to have the wound dressed. The tree is still there: five and a half metres round, thirty-four metres up, with the mottled white upper limbs an American sycamore shows once the outer bark flakes off. A bicentennial marker went in beside it in 1987. Worth saying plainly what a witness tree is and is not. Nothing in the wood records the battle. The claim rests on the tree's age and its position beside a house the wounded were brought into, and both of those are documented. The battlefield is a National Historic Landmark and the grounds are free to walk; the Gilpin house interior is timed guided tours only, Thursday to Sunday. The pin here marks the house rather than the trunk, because no tree-level fix exists, but the two stand within a yard of each other.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are down and the white upper limbs show

name: The Big Tree (Williamson Bur Oak)

location.address: Bur Oak Road, near McBaine, Boone County, Missouri

access: Free. Stands on privately owned farmland (the Williamson family, six generations) but is publicly accessible right beside Bur Oak Road, and the Katy Trail State Park rail-trail runs just yards away, making it a well known stop for cyclists. No fee found.
transport: Near McBaine, Boone County, Missouri, a few km from Columbia, MO. Not within 30 minutes of any city we currently publish; stands alone.
story: When Lewis and Clark came up the Missouri in 1804, this bur oak was already about two hundred years old. It is still standing in the river bottoms near McBaine: 7.3 metres around, 27 metres tall, a crown 40 metres across, tied as national champion of its species and Missouri's state champion since 1987. Sources put its start somewhere in the 1600s and its age between 350 and 400 years, with no ring count behind either figure. It has taken lightning strikes and sat through the floods of 1993 and 1995 that drowned much of this floodplain, and a professional arborist keeps an eye on it. In May 2026 COMO Magazine described it as about as healthy as a nearly four-century-old tree can be. The land belongs to the Williamson family and has for six generations, which means six generations have left it standing in the middle of good bottomland rather than in a fencerow. Boone County made it an official historic site in August 2021, the only tree in the county with that status. Bur Oak Road runs past it and the Katy Trail passes within yards, so cyclists have been stopping here for years without anyone organising it. Free, no gate, and you see it from the road before you reach it, because there is nothing else of that size in the field.

best_time.label: September and October, when the big fringed acorns drop into the field

name: Doerner Fir

location.address: BLM land off Upper East Fork Brummit Road, Coos County, Oregon, west of Roseburg
location.neighbourhood: Doerner Fir Trailhead, reached via a mostly-paved BLM forest road with a final 4.5 miles of gravel

access: Free, on BLM public land; short, well-marked trail from a dedicated trailhead parking lot. Access road is remote (about an hour of driving from Roseburg on paved and then gravel BLM roads) and not maintained in winter.
transport: No public transit; nearest town is Roseburg, OR, about an hour's drive.
story: In August 2025 a fire nobody has explained burned for several days in the crown of this Douglas fir, and the tree survived it. Firefighters put the blaze out. The fir lost roughly fifty feet off its top and with it the record it had held for years as the tallest known Douglas fir on Earth. Before the fire it measured 325.8 feet, 99.3 metres, which put it among the tallest trees anywhere that are not redwoods. The height on this page, about 84 metres, comes from press coverage after the fire rather than from a survey; nobody has run a tape up it since, so treat it as approximate until someone does. It is roughly 450 years old, give or take fifty, which made it a large tree long before the logging that took nearly everything around it. It was the Brummit Fir until it was renamed for a Douglas County commissioner. Getting there is an honest part of the trip: about an hour from Roseburg on BLM roads, the last four and a half miles gravel and not maintained through winter, then a short marked trail from a proper trailhead with a register to sign. What waits at the end is now a scarred survivor rather than a record holder, which is arguably the better reason to walk in.

name: Davie Poplar

location.address: McCorkle Place, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina
location.neighbourhood: McCorkle Place, the university's oldest quad, on public campus grounds

access: Free, open campus green space, no restrictions on approach.
transport: No public transit needed; on UNC's central Chapel Hill campus, walkable from downtown Chapel Hill.
story: The University of North Carolina stands where it does, campus legend says, because General William R. Davie fell asleep under this poplar in 1792 and decided the spot would do. That is a good story rather than a documented one, which is roughly the status of most things said about this tree. What can be measured: over 100 feet tall, over 16 feet around, and somewhere between 300 and 375 years old on the university's own estimate, which no ring count supports. Even at the low end of that band it is older than the university, and that is the only part of the legend that has to be true for the rest to be plausible. It stands on McCorkle Place, the oldest quad on campus, and UNC has spent a long time preparing for the day it goes. Davie Poplar Jr. was rooted from the original and grows a few steps away; Davie Poplar III came later. Both are separate trees, and the one people come for is the big one. Seeds from it were handed out to students in 2005, and the anniversary of that giveaway was still being written up in the campus paper twenty years later, which tells you how much weight a university can put on one tulip tree. The quad is open ground, free, crossed all day. In late October the crown turns clear yellow.

best_time.label: late October, when the crown turns clear yellow over the quad

name: Pando
age_estimate: estimated thousands of years (a single precise figure is disputed)

location.address: Old Spanish Trailhead, Highway 25 (Fishlake Scenic Byway), Fishlake National Forest, near Fish Lake, Utah
location.neighbourhood: the Old Spanish Trailhead parking area, where the Lakeshore National Recreation Trail runs a spur directly through the Pando clone

access: Free, US Forest Service land, no permit needed; a flat, easy 1.4-mile out-and-back trail from the Old Spanish Trailhead walks directly through the clone, and a further overlook is reachable via the Lakeshore National Recreation Trail off Forest Road 046N.
transport: No public transit; nearest town is Richfield, UT, about 25 minutes' drive.
story: Pando is not a tree. It is one quaking aspen: a single organism of roughly 40,000 stems sharing one root system across about 106 acres, commonly reckoned the most massive known living thing on Earth. Every stem is genetically identical, which is why the whole hillside changes colour in the same week each autumn, and why the trunks you walk between are closer to branches than to neighbours. Its age is a live argument rather than a rounded number. The popular figure is 80,000 years, derived from an assumed rate of spread. Other researchers put it anywhere from several hundred to about 14,000, and the disagreement is about method rather than about Pando. Nobody has settled it and we are not going to tidy it here. What is documented is that the clone is failing to replace itself: deer and cattle eat the young stems before they clear browsing height, so an organism of that age currently consists mostly of old wood, and the Forest Service manages it with that in mind. The Old Spanish Trailhead sits on Highway 25 by Fish Lake, free, no permit, and a flat 1.4 mile walk out and back goes straight into the clone. There is no single trunk to stand in front of and no way to see the whole of it at once. That is the thing you have come for.

best_time.label: late September into early October, when every stem turns gold in the same week

name: Colonel Armstrong

location.address: Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, 17000 Armstrong Woods Road, Guerneville, California
location.neighbourhood: Pioneer Trail, about 0.5 miles from the reserve entrance

access: Paid entry (California State Parks day-use vehicle fee, about $10); flat, easy walk on the reserve's main loop trail, roughly 0.5 miles from the parking lot.
transport: No public transit; Guerneville town centre is about a 5-minute drive.
story: This redwood is named after a lumberman, which sounds like an insult and is not. Colonel James B. Armstrong made his money cutting Sonoma County forest in the 1870s and 1880s and then set this stand aside rather than felling it, which is why about 1,400 years of tree is still standing half a mile up the trail from the entrance. It is the oldest named tree in the reserve and around 300 feet tall. Estimates run from roughly 1,200 to 1,600 years, so even at the cautious end it was two centuries old at the time of the Norman conquest. In August 2020 the Walbridge Fire reached this grove and crews worked to hold it. The reserve burned at its edges and the old trees came through, which is less luck than bark: a coast redwood carries a foot of it, low in resin and hard to light. Armstrong died in 1900 and the tree has put on another century since. Getting to it is easy in a way the size does not prepare you for. State Parks charges about ten dollars per vehicle for the day, the trail is flat, and it is a fifteen-minute stroll from the car park. It is evergreen and looks the same in February as in August, so the only thing worth timing is the crowd.

name: Parson Jones Tree

location.address: Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, 17000 Armstrong Woods Road, Guerneville, California
location.neighbourhood: near the reserve entrance, about 100 yards from the parking lot

access: Paid entry (California State Parks day-use vehicle fee, about $10); a very short, flat walk, about 100 yards from the parking lot.
transport: No public transit; Guerneville town centre is about a 5-minute drive.
story: The tallest tree here is also the closest to the car park, about a hundred yards in on flat ground. The Parson Jones Tree runs over 310 feet, some 94.5 metres, which makes it taller than Colonel Armstrong, the older and more visited of the two. That height comes from survey work in the 1970s and does not appear to have been redone, so the number is half a century old; a redwood of this age adds height slowly, which makes the figure more likely stale than wrong. Age estimates land near 1,300 years, in a band from about 1,100 to 1,500, none of it from a ring count. What the height means on the ground is a trunk that leaves your field of view and carries on. There is no point from which the top and the base are visible at once, which is why photographs of it are uniformly disappointing and why people end up standing there longer than they meant to. Same entrance and same ten dollar vehicle fee as Colonel Armstrong, which is five minutes further along the same flat loop. The pair takes well under an hour. This is the one visitors underestimate, because a tree that close to the road is assumed to be the warm-up rather than the tallest thing in the reserve.

name: The Emancipation Oak

location.address: Hampton University campus, near the corner of E Queen St and Tyler St, Hampton, VA

access: Free, on the open grounds of Hampton University's campus; part of the university's National Historic Landmark district.
transport: Within Hampton, VA. Not one of our currently published US cities; treat as its own place (Hampton, VA) unless a future pass opens a Hampton Roads/Norfolk-Virginia Beach city page it could join.
story: The Emancipation Proclamation got its first public reading in the South under this live oak, in September 1863, to the Black community of the Virginia Peninsula gathered in its shade. Before that, and before it was legal, Mary Peake taught freed and enslaved children to read under the same branches. The tree is still on the Hampton University campus and still used for ceremonies. Its canopy spreads about 98 feet across on a trunk barely 50 feet tall, which is what a live oak does when nothing crowds it: out rather than up. The age is genuinely unsettled. Older material says 150 to 200 years, a 2023 estimate says around 250, a 2022 report says 309. Nobody has cored it, deliberately, because taking a core from an old live oak to settle a number is a poor trade. Read it as somewhere between two and three centuries, and note that even the low end puts it here, and grown, in 1863. National Geographic once listed it among ten great trees of the world. It stands inside Hampton University's National Historic Landmark district, on open campus ground, free, with nothing between you and it. Most places where something like this happened keep a plaque. This one kept the tree that people were standing under.

name: The Peter Lebeck Oak

location.address: Fort Tejon State Historic Park, 4201 Fort Tejon Rd, Lebec, California

access: Free to view; Fort Tejon State Historic Park charges a day-use vehicle fee and is open daily 9am-4pm.
transport: Fort Tejon State Historic Park, Lebec, CA, on the west side of I-5 in Grapevine Canyon. About 113 km / 70 miles from Los Angeles (our nearest published city), roughly 1.5 hours drive, too far to count as a day-trip extension of LA.
story: In October 1837 a trapper called Peter Lebeck was killed by a grizzly bear here, and whoever buried him cut the notice into the bark of a valley oak: Peter le Beck, killed by a bear, Octr 17, 1837. By 1857 the tree had grown over the lettering and sealed it in. In the 1880s or 1890s the Foxtail Rangers, a group out of Bakersfield, cut that bark away and found the inscription mirrored on its underside, the tree having taken an impression of the words while healing over them. They re-marked the grave, and a headstone copying the wording went in during 1938. The recovered bark is on display, though sources disagree on whether at Fort Tejon itself or at the Kern County Museum in Bakersfield, so ask at the desk. The fort came seventeen years after the burial, in 1854, which makes the oak the older resident by some margin. Nobody has dated it properly. The most recent account we can point to is a 2016 visit describing the fort's valley oaks as around four hundred years old, so if you know better, or find this one changed, tell us. Fort Tejon State Historic Park sits beside I-5 in Grapevine Canyon, open daily from 9 to 4 with a day use vehicle fee, and the grave is part of an ordinary visit. The pin marks the park entrance rather than the tree.
